transcript:
This is NPR News now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Hurricane Isaias in the southwestern Gulf of Mexico has been brewing over unusually
warm waters for October.
Jessica Mazaros from member station WUSF reports on how climate change is influencing this
development.
The storm formed in an area of the Gulf that's at least three degrees warmer than average
for this time of year.
Shel Winkley, chief meteorologist for the nonprofit Climate Central, says the higher
temperature was made 300 to 800 times more likely due to global warming.
Some of these ocean temperatures in western Gulf would be almost virtually impossible
without the influence of human-caused climate change.
Not only does warm water intensify storms, it also creates more moisture.
The system is expected to drop four to six inches of rain along the Gulf Coast, with
even higher totals in localized spots.
For NPR News, I'm Jessica Mazaros in Tampa.
President Trump says the U.S. won't attack Iran before next month's midterm elections.
He announced it on social media today amid low public approval ratings over the economic
fallout from the U.S. war with Iran.
Private data have directly tied higher fuel prices and rising inflation to the war.
Vice President J.D. Vance is accusing the tech giant Microsoft of fraud at a White House
news conference.
Vance announced the Trump administration would suspend Microsoft from a program to apply
for green cards for employees who come to the U.S. to live and work on an H-1B visa.
For every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half
foreign indentured servants.
In a statement, Microsoft disputes the allegations, saying the vast majority of its workforce
in the U.S. is American.
Microsoft is a financial supporter of NPR.
Hundreds of police departments across the U.S. have real-time crime centers.
NPR's Meg Anderson reports privacy experts are worried those centers are increasingly
using AI.
Data like Axon Fusis is used in police command centers to pull in all kinds of data, from
license plate readers to body-worn cameras to surveillance video.
Police officers say the tool can help them monitor situations or find suspects almost
instantaneously.
But that is exactly what makes some privacy experts nervous.
Like Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a law professor at George Washington University.
That happens if there is a government that wants to silence a particular group or even
a particular person.
And you just built the architecture surveillance that makes that super easy.
Police told NPR they understand those concerns, but that the good outweighs the bad.
Axon did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Meg Anderson, NPR News.
Curtis Flowers, or this is NPR.
Curtis Flowers, a black man wrongfully imprisoned for more than 22 years for a quadruple murder
in Mississippi, has died.
Attorney Rob McDuff, with the Mississippi Center for Justice, tells the Associated Press that
Flowers' family confirmed he died yesterday at his home in Mississippi, but no cause of
death was disclosed.
He was 56.
Flowers was tried six times for the 1996 shooting deaths of four people.
At the last trial, he was sentenced to death.
The U.S. Supreme Court threw out his convictions and death sentence with a majority opinion
underscoring racial bias in jury selection.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh noted that District Attorney Doug Evans had removed 41 of 42 prospective
black jurors over the six trials.
The Water Utility Agency in Washington is saying the Potomac River has returned to normal
following a massive sewage spill earlier this year.
Research Station WAMU in Washington Jackson Cinnaburg reports.
DC Water declared that the Potomac River is healthy and has not suffered any lasting harm
from a break in the interceptor pipeline.
That sewage pipe broke in January, causing hundreds of millions of gallons of sewage
to spill into the river.
Following the break, tests found severely high levels of bacteria like E. coli downstream.
However, the E. coli warnings were lifted in August.
The testing now confirms other vitals like the levels of oxygen and nutrients in the
Potomac have also returned to normal.
For NPR News, I'm Jackson Cinnaburg in Washington.
U.S. stocks trading lower this hour with the NASDAQ down 378 points or 1.3 percent.
You're listening to NPR News.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now, sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism and get NPR Plus at plus.npr.org.
That's plus dot NPR dot org.

topics.text: Hurricane Isaias forms in unusually warm Gulf of Mexico waters influenced by climate change
President Trump says U.S. won't attack Iran before next month's midterm elections
Vice President Vance accuses Microsoft of fraud, suspends company from H-1B visa program
Privacy experts concerned about AI use in real-time crime centers across U.S. police departments
Curtis Flowers, wrongfully imprisoned 22 years for Mississippi quadruple murder, dies at 56
Washington water utility declares Potomac River healthy after massive January sewage spill
